TV statement: I voted for a pragmatic compromise because the real question was whether we would protect the programs that help people get good‑paying jobs or risk losing them chasing a perfect bill; this agreement closed part of a tax loophole while preserving and increasing funding for job training, apprenticeships, and supports that help local employers hire, and I pushed hard to keep those investments because our priority has to be teaching people skills and connecting them to real careers here at home. 

Op‑ed: I want to speak plainly to my neighbors about why I cast this vote: governing is about making choices that protect people today while we keep working to make tomorrow better, and in this case the choice was between walking away and risking the loss of vital job‑training and apprenticeship programs, or accepting a compromise that closed part of a tax loophole and, crucially, kept and strengthened investments that put people into careers and help small businesses find skilled workers; I chose to protect working families—because losing those programs would have been a real setback for people trying to climb into the middle class. The package was not perfect, and I will never pretend otherwise; some advocates rightly pushed for deeper changes, and I respect that push, but I also had to weigh the immediate consequences for people in our community who depend on training slots, apprenticeships and employer partnerships to learn new skills, get hired, and support their families. What we won matters in everyday terms: more funding for training programs, stronger apprenticeship grants, and safeguards that connect trainees with local employers so that training leads to a real paycheck—not just a certificate; these are the sorts of practical outcomes that change lives, and they were on the line during negotiations. During the process I fought to tighten loopholes where we could and to protect the worker‑facing pieces of the bill against pressure from well‑funded interests; critics who simplify that fight as “siding with lobbyists” leave out the full picture—that the final agreement did shrink a loophole and, more importantly, preserved and expanded programs that help people get into and advance in careers. My record shows I stand for investments in skills, for apprenticeships that open doors, and for small businesses that hire our neighbors; I will keep pushing to close remaining gaps and to ensure that future budget work builds on these wins so communities here get more opportunities, not fewer. If you want someone who will make tough choices to protect workers and local employers and then keep fighting to do better, that is what I will keep doing—straightforward, no spin, focused on results that matter to families in our towns.
